name: Tap water / fluoride avoidance

lead: Some appearance-focused people avoid tap water to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine, presenting it as part of a skin and health routine. Health bodies such as the WHO and CDC support fluoridation at recommended levels, while critics dispute its benefit and safety.
Fluoride is added to public water to reduce tooth decay, with a US recommended level of 0.7 mg/L. No study has tested whether avoiding fluoride changes how someone looks.

paras: People use home filters, bottled or spring water for drinking and cooking, and sometimes shower filters for washing. It is a permanent household switch rather than a short course.

Fluoridation's documented adverse effect at recommended levels is mostly mild dental fluorosis. Neurodevelopment concerns are debated, and a 2024 US court ruling addressed IQ risk. Reduced fluoride exposure is associated with more cavities in some reviews.

angle.text: Some appearance-focused users drink and wash with filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, aiming for healthier skin and teeth. Health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no study has looked at appearance.

wikipedia.title: Water supply and sanitation in the United States

lead: Tap water / fluoride avoidance is a practice in which people drink and sometimes wash with filtered, bottled, spring or distilled water instead of municipal tap water, mainly to avoid fluoride and sometimes chlorine, minerals or other additives. In appearance-focused communities it is presented as part of a routine aimed at keeping teeth, skin, hormones and overall health in good shape, so that the face and body look their best.[1][2]

The clearest appearance link is dental fluorosis, a change in tooth enamel caused by swallowing too much fluoride while teeth are forming. It ranges from faint white flecks to brown mottling and pitting, and the greatest risk is from birth to about age six.[3] Avoiding extra fluoride sources during those years is how some parents and adults frame the practice; after about age seven, most permanent teeth have finished developing and the risk falls substantially.[3]

Water fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to public supplies to reduce tooth decay; the US recommended level is 0.7 mg/L.[4][5] The WHO, FDI World Dental Federation and US CDC endorse it as safe and effective at recommended levels, while opponents argue the benefit is small, consent is lacking and safety is uncertain, and research on fluoride and children's IQ has drawn attention since 2024.[4][6][7][8] No published study has tested fluoride avoidance for facial appearance or skin.

paras: The practice usually means replacing tap water for drinking and cooking with bottled or spring water, with water from a home filter, or with distilled water, and sometimes switching to fluoride-free toothpaste. Practitioners cite avoiding fluoride and chlorine as the reason for choosing filtered or spring water.[1] Water filters in general work by sieving, adsorption, ion exchange or biofilms, and common household types include granular activated carbon filters and carbon block filters.[9]

Looksmaxxing posts tend to fold the idea into a broader purity routine: water that is free of additives, balanced hormones, clearer skin and healthy teeth are all named as hoped-for payoffs.[1][2] Some users go further, reporting that they distil their own water at home.[10] Others point out that bottled water is not necessarily cleaner, since plastic bottles are themselves a source of microplastics.[1][11]

Fluoride is added to public water mainly as sodium fluoride, fluorosilicic acid or sodium fluorosilicate; it does not change the water's taste, smell or look.[4] Grand Rapids, Michigan, began fluoridating on January 25, 1945, the first city to do so, after decades of research into the staining of teeth in areas with naturally fluoride-rich water.[4]

Some countries and cities, including Finland, Germany, Japan, the Netherlands and Switzerland, do not fluoridate or have stopped; Basel, for example, uses fluoridated salt.[4] Israel dropped mandatory fluoridation in 2014.[4][6]

The CDC says it does not mandate fluoridation; state and local governments decide whether to fluoridate, and voters often make that call. It calls fluoridation a cornerstone strategy for preventing cavities, says fluoridated water reduces cavities by about 25 percent in children and adults, and notes that the 0.7 mg/L US Public Health Service recommendation is not an enforceable standard.[5]

Opposition began soon after fluoridation started in the 1940s. The first large US controversy came in Wisconsin in 1950, and Rio Vista, California, fluoridated in 1951 and voted to remove its equipment in 1956.[6] In the 1950s and 1960s some far-right activists, including groups such as the John Birch Society, described fluoridation as a communist plot; by the mid-1960s that argument had lost influence, and the film Dr. Strangelove (1964) satirised it.[6]

Present-day opponents more often argue individual rights, informed consent, precaution and conflicts of interest, while proponents compare fluoridation to vaccination and food fortification and say it benefits those least able to pay for dental care.[6]

Wikipedia describes dental fluorosis as ranging from small chalky-white spots covering less than a quarter of a tooth, through whole-surface mottling and brown staining, to pitting in severe cases. Most cases are very mild or mild, and sources include naturally fluoride-rich water, certain crops and soil, and supplements; toothpaste is not strongly linked.[3]

Cosmetic options described include whitening for mild cases, microabrasion for moderate ones, and composite fillings, veneers or crowns for severe cases.[3] The 2024 Cochrane update of the water fluoridation review set out to evaluate the association of water fluoridation with dental fluorosis alongside its effect on cavities.[12] The previous Cochrane version estimated that about 12 percent of people at 0.7 ppm had fluorosis of aesthetic concern (95 percent CI 8 to 17 percent) and about 40 percent had fluorosis of any level, rating the evidence as low certainty.[8] A separate estimate quoted by Wikipedia is that fluoridation at 1 mg/L causes fluorosis in about one in six people and aesthetic concern in about one in 22.[7]

Wikipedia, citing CDC data, reports that about 41 percent of US adolescents have definite fluorosis and 20 percent questionable fluorosis, with very mild fluorosis rising from 17.2 to 28.5 percent between 1986 and 2014 and moderate-to-severe cases from 1.3 to 3.6 percent; about 90 percent of cases are mild or extremely mild.[3] Severity is graded with Dean's Index (0 to 5) or the finer TF Index (0 to 9).[3] Researchers suspect that several combined fluoride sources, such as water, toothpaste and varnishes, contribute to the rise, and the American Dental Association states that fluoridation is safe and effective and that fluorosis is usually mild.[3]

After the US Public Health Service lowered its recommended level in 2015, and after Hong Kong lowered its fluoridation by 0.2 ppm in 1978 with a reported 17 percent drop in cases, people who avoid fluoride point to such changes as showing the effect is dose-related.[3]

sections.h: Positions of health bodies and critics
paras: The WHO, FDI and US CDC endorse fluoridation, and the CDC named it one of the ten great public health achievements of the 20th century in 1999.[4][6][5] A 2015 Cochrane review estimated 35 percent fewer cavities in baby teeth and 26 percent in permanent teeth in children, but rated the evidence as low quality and found no conclusive adult research.[4][6][8]

The 2011 European Commission review saw no clear advantage over topical fluoride, and the 2007 Nuffield Council on Bioethics found good evidence for or against lacking.[4][6] Opponents raise consent, cost-effectiveness, precaution and conflict-of-interest arguments.[6] In September 2024 a US federal judge, Edward Chen, ruled in Food and Water Watch v. EPA that fluoridation posed an unreasonable risk of reduced IQ in children, requiring an EPA regulatory response.[6] A 2006 National Research Council report had earlier recommended lowering the US limit of 4 mg/L, which the EPA did not act on.[6]

Skeletal fluorosis results from long-term intake well above fluoridation levels and is endemic in parts of the Asian subcontinent; Wikipedia calls dental fluorosis the only generally accepted adverse effect at the levels used for fluoridation.[7] Research on neurodevelopment has grown more prominent. A 2024 US HHS National Toxicology Program monograph concluded that water fluoride above 1.5 mg/L is associated with lower IQ in children.[7]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis in JAMA Pediatrics pooled 74 studies, mostly from China, and found that higher fluoride exposure was associated with lower IQ; the association for drinking water was null below 1.5 mg/L, and each 1 mg/L rise in urinary fluoride was linked to a 1.63-point IQ decrease, or 1.14 points in low risk-of-bias studies.[8] The authors noted uncertainty for concentrations below 1.5 mg/L.[8] Fluoridation advocates and critics read these results differently, with critics citing the dose-response pattern and advocates citing the null finding at levels used in fluoridation.[6][8]

Some people who avoid tap water are also reacting to chlorine or mineral content. Wikipedia reports that hard drinking water may increase childhood eczema prevalence, though water softeners did not reduce symptoms once the condition was established, and that hard water reduces soap lathering.[13] These points concern minerals, not fluoride.

People who avoid tap water also name microplastics. A 2024 review reports that a global study found up to 83 percent of tap water samples contained microplastic fibres and that ingested particles have been associated with harmful effects in animals, raising concerns about human outcomes.[11] Bottled-water drinkers are not exempt from the concern, since forum posters note that plastic bottles are a source of microplastics too.[1][11] These other concerns have not been linked in published studies to appearance.

Dental fluorosis is the only clear adverse effect at recommended levels. Little effect on fracture risk and no clear link to cancer has been reported, and rare acute poisonings have followed improper dosing, including a fatal 1992 Alaska outbreak.[4] Wikipedia notes the 2006 National Research Council found fracture evidence suggestive but inadequate at 2 mg/L.[7]

Looksmax.org has threads asking whether tap water is harmful and listing what users say is in it.[1][2] In one, the poster says that people who worry about tap water phytoestrogens still buy bottled water, which he says degrades into microplastics, and asks which is worse; a reply says it depends on whether you live in Europe or North America.[1] In another, a poster who drinks several litres a day from a village well asks whether it is a problem, while replies show the thread turning into banter about appearance.[2]

A longer thread titled as an experiment describes a user who distilled London tap water and photographed the residue, reading it as evidence of metals, hormones, drugs and sediment in the supply; the poster ties this to a belief that the water company would not disclose what it adds.[10] Others in these communities link water quality to hormone balance, which is why phytoestrogens appear in posts.[1][10] Published sources do not link fluoride avoidance to facial appearance; hard water, by comparison, is described by Wikipedia as dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals.[13]

No studies found on fluoride avoidance and facial appearance. Studies of water fluoridation concern dental and general health outcomes, summarised above.[4][6][12] The 2024 Cochrane update of the fluoridation-and-caries review, searching databases to August 2023, set out to assess the effects of starting or stopping community water fluoridation on tooth decay and the association of fluoridation with dental fluorosis, using prospective controlled studies of fluoridated versus non-fluoridated or naturally low-fluoride populations; it found all included studies were non-randomised.[12][8]

lore.intro: Tap-water avoidance on looksmaxxing forums is mostly framed around general purity, hormones, filters, bottled versus spring water and microplastics, with fluoride one of several named concerns.[1][2][10]

claims.claim: Tap water contains fluoride and other additives that are harmful, so filtered or spring water is better.
Fluoride lowers IQ and harms development, so avoiding it protects the brain and body.
Fluoride exposure in childhood stains and spots teeth, so avoiding it keeps teeth looking better.
Bottled water is no better than tap because plastic bottles release microplastics.
Hard or treated tap water harms skin.
Water companies add hormones, metals and drugs that residue from distilled tap water reveals.
